claims.text: The baseline material is a single-phase, homogenized high-entropy alloy with a uniform microstructure and no significant secondary-phase precipitates.
Minor dopant additions can selectively trigger formation of a metastable secondary phase in a high-entropy alloy.
The dopant-induced phase can be introduced without changing grain size.
The induced secondary phase consists of metastable precipitates, potentially including transformable hcp particles.
Metastable precipitates transform under mechanical loading.
Transformation of metastable particles activates crack deflection.
Transformation of metastable particles activates crack bridging.
Transformation of metastable particles activates micro-cracking as an extrinsic toughening mechanism.
The particle-transformation and crack-shielding mechanisms delay crack propagation and maintain or enhance toughness.
The proposed transformation-toughening behavior remains effective under high strain rate and elevated-temperature loading.
A critical metastable-precipitate volume fraction governs the transition between brittle behavior and enhanced toughness.
Variants exceeding the critical precipitate-volume-fraction threshold will have significantly higher SENB-measured fracture toughness than the homogeneous baseline alloy.
Variants below the critical precipitate-volume-fraction threshold will lose toughness and exhibit a brittle response.
The undoped homogeneous baseline has lower fracture toughness because it lacks a significant volume fraction of metastable precipitates.
The hypothesis applies only in a narrow compositional window without grain-size changes or competing-phase formation.
The proposed behavior is particularly applicable when lattice-distortion and dislocation-interaction effects are minimized.
Failure to observe a statistically significant toughness enhancement as precipitate volume fraction increases would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction allows precipitate increases below a critical threshold to reduce toughness, whereas the falsification rule says that an increase in precipitate volume fraction without toughness enhancement falsifies the hypothesis. The rule does not restrict falsification to samples above the proposed threshold.
